Dog Bites in Washington: When You Can Sue, and the One Defense That Beats It

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·9 min read·October 13, 2026

A dog you have walked past a hundred times came off a porch and took hold of your daughter's face. You are in an urgent care waiting room, somebody has handed you a phone number for animal control, and that evening a claims adjuster for the owner's insurance company calls and is very pleasant. Washington's dog bite statute is unusually favorable to the person who was bitten. The single question that decides most of these cases is one you may already have answered out loud to that adjuster.

Washington has no one bite rule

In many states you have to prove the owner knew the dog was dangerous, which usually means proving it had bitten somebody before. Washington does not work that way. RCW 16.08.040(1) makes the owner of a dog that bites a person liable for the damages the bitten person suffers, and then adds the clause that matters: "regardless of the former viciousness of such dog or the owner's knowledge of such viciousness."

A dog with a spotless history, a dog that has never growled at anyone, an owner who is genuinely shocked. None of that is a defense to a bite. Liability is strict, which moves the fight off whether the owner did anything wrong and onto two different questions: were you lawfully where you were standing, and did you provoke the dog.

There is one carve-out in the statute itself. RCW 16.08.040(2) says the section does not apply to the lawful application of a police dog. A police dog deployment is a different case, usually an excessive force claim under the Fourth Amendment rather than a dog bite claim, and it runs on different rules and different deadlines.

Where you were standing when it happened

The statute covers a bite in a public place, and a bite on private property if you were lawfully there, including on the dog owner's own property. A delivery driver on the walkway, a guest in the kitchen, a child in a front yard she was invited into: all lawfully present.

RCW 16.08.050 defines lawful presence as being on the property "with the express or implied consent of the owner," and then attaches a proviso that does real work: consent "shall not be presumed when the property of the owner is fenced or reasonably posted." A fence or a sign does not end the claim. It removes the assumption that you were welcome and puts you to proving you were invited.

So the first thing worth writing down is the geography. Which side of the fence you were on, whether the gate was open, whether there was a sign and what it actually said, whether you had been there before and at whose invitation. Photograph the fence line and the sign the same week, because both change.

Provocation is a complete defense, and that is what the adjuster is asking about

RCW 16.08.060 is a single sentence: "Proof of provocation of the attack by the injured person shall be a complete defense to an action for damages." Complete, not partial. Provocation does not reduce the claim the way ordinary comparative fault does. It ends it.

That is why the friendly early phone call matters so much. Was she playing with him. Did she grab his tail. Had she been teasing him through the fence before. Those are not small talk. A recorded answer given on day one by a frightened parent, or by a seven-year-old, gets read back a year later in a deposition.

What counts as provocation is a question of fact, and with young children it is heavily contested, because a child doing what children do around animals is not the same thing as a person tormenting a dog. Say what happened accurately and stop there. Nothing obliges you to give a recorded statement to the dog owner's insurer. A policy you bought yourself is different, because it usually carries a duty to cooperate.

A bite is not the only way a dog hurts someone, and the statute only covers bites

RCW 16.08.040 is built around the word bite. A great deal of real dog injury is not a bite. A large dog that jumps up and knocks an older person onto a sidewalk. A dog that bolts into the road and causes a collision. A dog that attacks another dog, with the owner hurt trying to pull them apart. A dog that chases a cyclist into a ditch.

Those are ordinary negligence claims, and they are harder, because negligence puts the owner's knowledge back in issue: what the owner knew or should have known about this particular dog, whether the restraint was adequate, whether a local leash ordinance was broken. Washington recognizes both routes, and a careful claim often pleads the statute and negligence together, so that an argument about whether teeth actually broke skin does not end everything.

Injury to another dog is handled as damage to property plus veterinary cost, which lands badly on people who think of a dog as family. It is better to know that going in than to find it out from an adjuster.

Dog attack laws in Washington: dangerous dog and potentially dangerous dog

RCW 16.08.070 defines a potentially dangerous dog as one that, unprovoked, bites a person or a domestic animal, or chases or approaches a person in public "in a menacing fashion or apparent attitude of attack." A dangerous dog is one that inflicts severe injury on a person without provocation, kills a domestic animal off the owner's property, or bites again after already having been found potentially dangerous with notice to the owner. Severe injury has a hard definition in the same section: "broken bones or disfiguring lacerations requiring multiple sutures or cosmetic surgery."

Those designations drive restraint and criminal exposure rather than your damages. RCW 16.08.090(1) makes it unlawful for the owner of a dangerous dog to let it outside its proper enclosure unless it is muzzled and held on a substantial chain or leash by a responsible person, and RCW 16.08.100 provides for confiscation, destruction in some circumstances, and criminal penalties reaching a class C felony. RCW 16.08.090(3) also lists who cannot trigger a dangerous dog declaration at all, including a person committing a willful trespass or another tort on the owner's premises, a person tormenting or abusing the dog, and a person committing a crime.

The reason this still matters to a civil claim is evidence. An animal control file can hold a prior potentially dangerous designation, a neighbor's complaint from two years ago, or an earlier bite report, and all of it bears on the negligence theory and on what a jury thinks the owner should have known. Request the file early. Agencies purge records and witnesses move.

Can I sue my neighbor for a dog bite, and who actually pays?

The defendant is the owner. RCW 16.08.070(7) defines owner broadly, reaching any person or entity "possessing, harboring, keeping, having an interest in, or having control or custody of" the animal, but that definition applies by its own terms only to RCW 16.08.070 through 16.08.100, the dangerous dog sections. RCW 16.08.040 does not carry its own definition, so whether a person who was keeping the dog but did not own it is liable for the bite is a question to sort out early rather than assume.

In practice the money is homeowner's or renter's liability insurance, and the insurer both defends the owner and writes the check. Two things are worth checking before anybody assumes there is coverage. Some policies exclude particular breeds or exclude animal liability outright, and the owner often does not know that. And a landlord is not automatically on the hook for a tenant's dog, which takes showing the landlord knew about this dog's dangerous propensity and had some control over whether it stayed.

If the dog belongs to a city, a county, a school district, or the state, a separate statute controls what you have to do before you can sue at all, and missing that step ends a strong case. That is covered in the article on claims against government entities.

How long you have to bring a dog bite claim in Washington

Three years. A personal injury claim runs under RCW 4.16.080(2), which sets a three-year limit for "any other injury to the person or rights of another," and the clock starts at the injury.

For a child the clock runs differently. RCW 4.16.190 excludes from the limitation period the time a claimant was under eighteen, so a five-year-old's claim is not gone at eight. That is not a reason to wait. Scars mature and change, witnesses move away, the dog is rehomed or euthanized, and photographs taken in the first week are worth more than any later description of what the wound looked like.

Three years is the outer boundary, not the plan. Nobody can value an injury before treatment is far enough along to know what the permanent part of it is.

Where this goes wrong

The recorded statement given on day one, before anybody has slept, which locks in a version of events that a careful account would have stated differently.

No photographs of the wound before it closed, and none of the property. A healed scar photographs as a thin line. The same injury at seventy-two hours does not.

Medical records that never use the word dog. Urgent care charts a laceration, the follow-up charts a wound check, and eighteen months later there is no document tying the injury to the animal.

Treating the owner as the adversary. The adversary is the insurer. The owner is frequently a neighbor you still have to live beside, and the claim is against a policy they pay for precisely so this can be handled without a feud.

Taking the first offer before a plastic surgery consult. Scarring is the category most often undervalued, and scarring on a child's face is frequently permanent. A consult that prices revision surgery over the years ahead is what puts the future cost of the injury into the claim instead of leaving it out.

Assuming a fence or a sign ends it. Under RCW 16.08.050 it changes what has to be proved. It does not decide the case.

What a lawyer does here

Most of the work is early and unglamorous. Getting the animal control and law enforcement file before it ages. Finding the policy and reading its exclusions. Documenting the scene and the wound while both still show what happened. Keeping you off the phone with the adjuster. Getting the right treating specialist to say, in writing, what this injury will mean in ten years. Somebody also has to tell you honestly when provocation is a real problem in your case instead of a bluff, because that answer changes what the claim is worth.
